title: This week in Content Lab
lede: Five posts that worked and exactly why, how to make your own, and what clients are searching for right now.

trends.intro: Hair searches rising on Pinterest right now. These are the words clients search with, so using them in captions and on-screen text can help your posts show up when they look.

source.name: Pinterest Trends, US, data through Nov 6, 2026

trends.takeaway: Softer, darker, lower-maintenance color is climbing into winter.

ideas.title: Your unpopular opinion
ideas.principle: People are drawn to someone speaking their mind. When they agree, it validates what they already think, so they like it and send it on.
dissection: The hook
A microphone held up to a stylist with one question on screen: "What's your unpopular hair opinion?" You want to hear the answer before she says it.
The format

One take after another, a sentence or two each: bangs aren't for everyone, layers can make thin hair look thinner, short hair isn't lower maintenance. Big word-by-word captions and a small photo for each point. The setting keeps moving too: stylists cutting, washing, stocking shelves.
Why people stayed
Every take is something clients believe and stylists have opinions on. Each new answer resets the curiosity: what's the next one?
Why people engaged
Agreement. The top comment, liked by over a thousand people, says the short-hair take is true. Being validated is why they liked and shared it.
ideas.concept: Say the hair opinion you'd actually stand behind, one you've watched play out in your chair. Opinions about hair and products only, never about other stylists.
ideas.hook: What's my unpopular hair opinion? Short hair is more work than long hair.
ideas.hook2: Three hair opinions I'll stand behind, even if you won't like them.
steps: Write three opinions you genuinely hold from your own clients, each one sentence plus the reason: "Blunt bangs can age a face. Here's why."
Phone at eye level at your station. Read the question on screen, then answer each one in under ten seconds. Add big captions.
Caption: "Agree or disagree?" Reply to the first comments, especially the ones that disagree, without arguing.

ref.headline: A salon team, one mic, one question
ref.desc: A salon filmed its stylists answering "what's your unpopular hair opinion?" one after another. About 50 seconds.

shots: Solo: you at your station, eye level, one take per clip
Team: someone off camera holds the phone or a mic up to each stylist in turn
Optional: a photo for each point (the bang, the bob) dropped in the corner
structure: Take two, take three (one breath each)
talking: One sentence for the opinion, one for the reason
Say it like you'd say it to a client, not like a lecture
No digs at other stylists, salons or clients
guide.caption: "Agree or disagree?" plus the take you'd defend hardest. Reply to disagreement with your reason, not an argument.
adapt: Blonding: "Toning every visit isn't always needed"
Cutting: "Face-framing layers aren't for every face"
Salon owner: ask each stylist on your team the question

ideas.title: Raw lift
ideas.principle: Show the stage nobody posts and say what it tells you. Honest work, explained, is what people trust.
dissection: The hook
Foils being peeled off one after another at the bowl, from above. Foil pulls are satisfying to watch.
The format
Foils out, a slow brush through the wet raw blonde, then a cut straight to the finished hair at 16 seconds. Under 20 seconds.
What made it different
The caption said the foil work was so good they left it all as raw lift. No toner. Most stylists wouldn't show untoned lift, let alone leave it.
Why it beat her usual
About 27 times her normal views. You get the satisfying process and a gorgeous finished blonde, with no toner at all. Viewers see the work hold up.
ideas.concept: Film your lift straight out of the foils and say what you see: clean or not, even or not, whether it needs toner and why. The insight is the content.
ideas.hook: Straight out of the foils. No toner yet. Here's what I'm looking at.
ideas.hook2: This is the part most stylists never post.
steps: Phone above the bowl. Film the foils coming out, fast, 5 seconds.
Brush through the raw lift slowly and say, or write, one thing it tells you: even from root to ends, no banding, or exactly why it still needs a gloss.
Cut to the finished hair, 3 seconds. Caption: what you were aiming for at this stage.

ref.headline: Foils out, raw blonde, no toner
ref.desc: A blonde specialist filmed foils coming out, a brush through the raw lift, then the finished hair. Under 20 seconds.

shots: Overhead at the bowl, foils coming out
A slow brush-through along the part
structure: Brush-through + one line of what you see (5–15s)
talking: Say what you see in plain words: "even lift, no hot roots"
If it needs toner, say why; that's the insight
Don't call it perfect; show it
guide.caption: One line on what the raw stage told you, then the gloss or toner you chose (or didn't).
adapt: Brunette lightening: show the raw level before the gloss and why you're keeping warmth
Gray blending: the lift on the gray before blending
Lived-in blonde: how your teasing shows up in the raw lift

ideas.title: Real hair only
ideas.principle: Name a frustration every stylist shares, then answer it with your real work. People share what they've felt too.
dissection: The hook
The caption names something every stylist has felt lately: clients bringing inspiration photos that are AI.
The format
Photos of one real client's bobs over several years. Beautiful work, and the point is that every photo is real.
Why it worked
It's relatable. Stylists comment that they can't find real inspo either. The idea carries the post, not the photography.
Honest note
Small numbers for a still post, about twice her usual likes. Included for the idea, which is timely and works for every stylist.
ideas.concept: Post a real client's hair in good daylight and say plainly that it's real, with what it takes to keep: weeks between visits, minutes to style.
ideas.hook: Half the inspo photos I get now are AI. This is real hair, on a real client.
ideas.hook2: Bring me this one. It's a real person, and I can actually do it.
steps: Photograph a finished client in daylight from two or three angles. No filters, no smoothing.
First slide: your best photo with "real client, no filter".
Last slide: how she keeps it, weeks between visits and minutes to style. Caption: your AI-inspo line in your own words.

ref.headline: Real photos in an AI-inspo world
ref.desc: A colorist posted photos of one client's real bobs over the years, with a caption about clients bringing AI inspiration photos.
ref.numbers: About 2× her usual likes for a still post

shots: Front, side and back in daylight
Optional: the same client a few months later, if you have it
structure: Slide 1: best photo + "real client, no filter"
Last slide: upkeep in two lines
talking: Say it in first person: "the inspo I get", not "you should"
No dig at AI users; just show what's real
guide.caption: Your line about AI inspo, then one sentence on what this hair takes to maintain. Invite clients to save it for their consult.
adapt: Blonding: a real lived-in blonde at week 8, not just day one
Cutting: the same cut at 6 weeks
Extensions: how they look after a month of real life

ideas.title: Wet vs dry
ideas.principle: Show the moment that worries clients, then the moment that relieves them. Wanting to see the "after" keeps people watching.
dissection: The hook
Wet hair being combed through with "Wet" on screen. It looks dark and flat, which is exactly what makes clients panic at the bowl.
The format
Six seconds wet, then a straight cut to the same client dry and styled, labelled "Dry", visibly lighter and brighter. Fifteen seconds, no talking.
Why people stayed
Anticipation: you want to see how light it really dries. The jump from dark to bright is the payoff.
Why it beat her usual
Several times her normal reels, with over 10K likes. It answers a question every color client has, so people save it and send it.
ideas.concept: Film the same color twice: wet at the bowl, then dry and styled at the mirror, from the same side. Label each. Let the difference do the talking.
ideas.hook: Wet vs dry. Don't panic at the bowl.
ideas.hook2: This is why I tell you not to judge it wet.
steps: At the bowl after toning, comb the hair flat and film 5 seconds from the side. Text: "Wet".
After styling, film the same side, same distance, 5 seconds of movement. Text: "Dry".
Caption: one line on why color reads darker wet (water darkens it) and that this is normal.

ref.headline: Wet, then dry
ref.desc: A blonde specialist filmed the same client wet at the bowl, then dry and styled, each labelled. 15 seconds, no talking.

shots: Side view at the bowl, hair combed flat, wet
Same side, same distance, dry and styled, a little movement
talking: If you add text, keep it to the two labels and one reassuring line
guide.caption: "Wet = darker, dry = lighter" in your own words, plus one line for clients who panic at the bowl.
adapt: Brunette: wet looks almost black, dry shows the dimension
Copper: wet reads deeper and redder, dry shows the true tone
Extensions: wet shows the blend lines, dry shows how they disappear
Gray blending: wet looks flat, dry shows the soft blend

ideas.title: Hair I did today (with prices)
ideas.principle: People are nosy about what things cost. Showing your real day, with real prices, answers a question everyone wants answered.
dissection: The hook
The stylist on camera with the title "Hair I did today as a lived-in color specialist (with prices)". You stay to see the numbers.
The format
Each client's finished hair, one after another, each labelled with the client number, the service and the price. About 30 seconds.
Why people stayed
Curiosity about prices and what a stylist actually does in a day. Each new client resets it: what's the next one, what did it cost?
Why it works for everyone
It's a common format, but every stylist's day is different, so every remake is different.
ideas.concept: At the end of a normal day, post each client's finished hair with the service name and price. Your work, your prices, your day.
ideas.hook: Hair I did today as a [your specialty], with prices.
ideas.hook2: What a Tuesday behind the chair actually looks like, prices included.
steps: Through the day, film or photograph each finished client for 3–4 seconds.
Open on you, 3 seconds, with the title on screen.
Cut through each client with one label: service + price. End on a line like "which was your favorite?"

ref.headline: Today's clients, with prices
ref.desc: A lived-in color specialist posted each client's finished hair from one day, labelled with the service and the price.

shots: Each client's finished hair, 3–4 seconds each, same spot and light if you can
talking: Let the labels talk; no voiceover needed
Use the service names clients would actually book
guide.caption: Your specialty, your city, and an invitation to book. Prices match your menu.
adapt: Cutting: "cuts I did today, with prices"
Extensions: method, rows and price per client
Newer stylists: "what I charge at year two" builds trust too
